newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain, Italy yields won't decouple soon - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Spain, Italy yields won't decouple soon - analysts.

text.p: Spanish and Italian assets will stay in a tight range in the short run, despite European Commission forecasts putting Spain on track for a timely entry into Europe's single currency with Italy missing out, analysts said on Thursday.
This is because the market believes the outlook painted by the report is provisional, and is convinced that the decision on entry into the euro will be a political one.

The European Commission said on Wednesday that Spain's public deficit to gross domestic product ratio is likely to be around three percent this year, while its Italian counterpart will stand at 3.2 percent.
"It seems the markets are not reflecting such a view," said Antonio Garcia Rebollar, director at Renta 4 brokerage.
At around 1430 GMT the 10-year spread between Italian BTPs and Spanish bonos was trading at around 77 basis points from 70 basis points on Wednesday.
Despite some economic differences between the two countries, analysts said a decoupling in yields, if any, will take place only longer term.
"We can see a trend towards decoupling between Italy and Spain longer term, but short term I expect little changes," said Felix Gonzalez, chief economist at Beta Capital brokerage.
Analysts stressed also that final decisions on which countries enter EMU first will be a political choice.
"At the end there will be strong political arguments bringing France and German to back Italy's entrance," said Xavier Segura, chief economist at Caja de Cataluna.
Though analysts gave less credibility to the EU report regarding Italy, they said it provided strong support for Spain's market.
"The data published yesterday by the European Commission are among the best ones Spain has ever had for its entry into EMU," said Felix Garcia.
Analysts' forecasts of further reduction in inflation make the EU Commission's predictions even more likely.
"Before the summer, inflation will continue to fall. In May the CPI could be around 1.5 percent and by then people could see differences between Italy and Spain," said Garcia.
But Italy is also showing a tamer pattern in its inflation trend.
According the latest harmonised CPI, February data showed a yearly rate at 2.5 percent for Spain and at 2.3 percent for Italy.
